name: Keycloak
tagline: Issues signed tokens for SSO: OIDC, realms, clients and roles.

howItWorks.title: Authorization Code flow with PKCE
howItWorks.body:
The app redirects the browser to Keycloak with a code_challenge (S256).
The user logs in once; Keycloak redirects back with a one-time code.
The app swaps code plus code_verifier for tokens at the token endpoint.
Other apps in the realm reuse the session cookie: that is SSO.

howItWorks.title: Realms, clients, roles
howItWorks.body:
A realm is an isolated space of users, clients, roles and policy.
A client is an app that may ask for tokens; public clients use PKCE.
Realm and client roles are mapped into token claims.
Mappers add audience and custom claims.

howItWorks.title: JWT validation
howItWorks.body:
Fetch the realm JWKS and verify the signature by kid.
Check iss equals the realm URL, aud contains your API, exp is in the future.
Allow a small clock skew, such as 30 seconds.
Cache the JWKS; refresh on an unknown kid.

howItWorks.title: HA with Infinispan
howItWorks.body:
Nodes form one Infinispan cluster; discovery uses the database (jdbc-ping).
Distributed caches hold sessions and auth sessions across nodes.
All nodes share one PostgreSQL for users, clients and realms.
Open TCP 7800 and 57800 between nodes. JBoss grouping works the same way, via JGroups.

howItWorks.title: Realm import, export and heap
howItWorks.body:
kc.sh export writes a realm to JSON; start --import-realm loads it.
Stop the node before a full export, or use a separate instance.
Set JAVA_OPTS_KC_HEAP to bound the JVM heap.
Size the container limit above heap for metaspace and threads.

howItWorks.title: What sits in front
howItWorks.body:
Users (Users layer) open a browser to the Keycloak hostname over HTTPS.
A reverse proxy or load balancer in the Edge layer usually fronts it; common modes are re-encrypt and passthrough.
Limit network access so only the proxy reaches Keycloak.
Set the public hostname so issuer URLs match what clients see.

howItWorks.title: What sits behind
howItWorks.body:
A relational database holds users, clients and realms; PostgreSQL is a standard choice.
Optional federation reads users from LDAP or Active Directory.
Other Keycloak nodes join the same Infinispan cluster for sessions.
On Kubernetes (Platform), the Keycloak Operator runs it and an Ingress exposes it.

howItWorks.title: Apps and APIs
howItWorks.body:
Apps are OIDC clients; single-page and mobile apps use a public client with PKCE.
An API or gateway validates JWTs offline with the realm JWKS, or calls the introspection endpoint.
The Kubernetes API server can trust the realm as an OIDC issuer for kubectl logins.
Gateways such as Kong validate tokens before traffic reaches services.

howItWorks.title: Tokens
howItWorks.body:
An access token is short-lived and carries claims for the API.
A refresh token obtains a new access token without another login.
An ID token tells the app who signed in.
All are signed with the realm key and verified through the JWKS.

howItWorks.title: Alternatives
howItWorks.body:
Authentik: choose it for a lighter, Python-based self-hosted identity provider.
Auth0 or Okta: choose them when a hosted SaaS should run identity.
Amazon Cognito: choose it when the stack already lives in AWS.
Microsoft Entra ID: choose it when users already live in Microsoft 365.

flow: The user opens the app; it has no session.
The app redirects the browser to the realm auth endpoint with a PKCE challenge.
The load balancer picks a node; Keycloak shows the login page.
The user authenticates; Keycloak stores the session in Infinispan.
Keycloak redirects back to the app with a one-time code.
The app posts code plus code_verifier to the token endpoint.
Keycloak returns access, refresh and ID tokens signed with the realm key.
The API checks signature, issuer, audience and exp, then serves the request.

deploy.summary: Bring up a hardened Linux host, run Keycloak under systemd, then add a node.
prerequisites: TLS certificate for the public hostname
DNS name pointing at the load balancer

steps.title: SSH keys, static IP, firewall
steps.code:
ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub <USER>@<NODE_IP>   # then set PasswordAuthentication no in sshd_config.d
# netplan: addresses: [<NODE_IP>/24], routes via <GW>, nameservers <DNS_IP>
sudo netplan apply
# DNS: sso.example.com A <LB_IP>  (placeholder)
sudo ufw allow 8443/tcp
sudo ufw allow from <PEER_NODE_IP> to any port 7800,57800 proto tcp
steps.note: 8443 serves users. 7800 and 57800 are for the cluster, so open them to peers only.

steps.title: Install Keycloak 26.0.7
steps.code:
sudo apt-get install -y openjdk-21-jre-headless
curl -LO https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/releases/download/26.0.7/keycloak-26.0.7.tar.gz
sudo tar -xzf keycloak-26.0.7.tar.gz -C /opt && sudo ln -s /opt/keycloak-26.0.7 /opt/keycloak
sudo useradd -r -s /usr/sbin/nologin keycloak && sudo chown -R keycloak: /opt/keycloak-26.0.7
steps.note: Create a PostgreSQL database and user named keycloak first.

steps.title: Configure and run under systemd
steps.code:
# /opt/keycloak/conf/keycloak.conf
db=postgres
db-url=jdbc:postgresql://<DB_HOST>:5432/keycloak
db-username=keycloak
db-password=<DB_PASSWORD>
hostname=https://sso.example.com
https-port=8443
https-certificate-file=/etc/keycloak/tls.crt
https-certificate-key-file=/etc/keycloak/tls.key
health-enabled=true
metrics-enabled=true

# /etc/systemd/system/keycloak.service
[Unit]
After=network-online.target
[Service]
User=keycloak
Environment=JAVA_OPTS_KC_HEAP="-Xms1g -Xmx2g"
Environment=KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_USERNAME=admin KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD=<ADMIN_PASSWORD>
ExecStart=/opt/keycloak/bin/kc.sh start
Restart=on-failure
[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
steps.note: Two files in one block. Then daemon-reload and enable --now keycloak.

steps.title: Create realm, client, role and user
steps.code:
K=/opt/keycloak/bin/kcadm.sh
$K config credentials --server https://sso.example.com:8443 --realm master --user admin
$K create realms -s realm=lab -s enabled=true
$K create clients -r lab -s clientId=web -s publicClient=true -s 'redirectUris=["https://app.example.com/*"]' -s 'attributes."pkce.code.challenge.method"=S256'
$K create roles -r lab -s name=editor
$K create users -r lab -s username=alice -s enabled=true
$K set-password -r lab --username alice --new-password '<USER_PASSWORD>'
steps.note: The client is public and forces S256 PKCE. Add an audience mapper so access tokens carry aud for your API.

steps.title: Run the PKCE flow
steps.code:
V=$(openssl rand -base64 48 | tr '+/' '-_' | tr -d '=\n')
C=$(printf %s "$V" | openssl dgst -sha256 -binary | openssl base64 -A | tr '+/' '-_' | tr -d '=')
echo "https://sso.example.com:8443/realms/lab/protocol/openid-connect/auth?client_id=web&response_type=code&scope=openid&redirect_uri=https://app.example.com/cb&code_challenge=$C&code_challenge_method=S256&state=xyz"
# log in, copy ?code= from the redirect
curl -s https://sso.example.com:8443/realms/lab/protocol/openid-connect/token -d grant_type=authorization_code -d client_id=web -d code=<CODE> -d redirect_uri=https://app.example.com/cb -d code_verifier="$V"
steps.note: Open the printed URL in a browser. The code is single-use and short-lived.

steps.title: Validate the JWT in an API
steps.code:
import jwt  # pip install 'pyjwt[crypto]==2.9.0'
url = 'https://sso.example.com:8443/realms/lab/protocol/openid-connect/certs'
key = jwt.PyJWKClient(url).get_signing_key_from_jwt(token).key
claims = jwt.decode(token, key, algorithms=['RS256'],
    audience='<API_AUDIENCE>', issuer='https://sso.example.com:8443/realms/lab', leeway=30)
steps.note: The issuer must match the public hostname exactly. leeway=30 allows 30 seconds of clock skew.

steps.title: Export and import realms
steps.code:
sudo systemctl stop keycloak
sudo -u keycloak /opt/keycloak/bin/kc.sh export --dir /var/backups/kc --realm lab --users realm_file
sudo cp /var/backups/kc/lab-realm.json /opt/keycloak/data/import/
sudo -u keycloak /opt/keycloak/bin/kc.sh start --import-realm
steps.note: Import skips realms that already exist. Run it on the target node, not the live one.

steps.title: Add a second node for HA
steps.code:
# same keycloak.conf and the same database as node 1
echo 'cache=ispn' | sudo tee -a /opt/keycloak/conf/keycloak.conf
echo 'cache-stack=jdbc-ping' | sudo tee -a /opt/keycloak/conf/keycloak.conf
sudo systemctl edit keycloak   # add: Environment=JAVA_OPTS_APPEND="-Djgroups.bind.address=<NODE2_IP>"
sudo systemctl enable --now keycloak
steps.note: Repeat on node 1 with its own IP. Put both behind HAProxy or NGINX health-checking /health/ready on port 9000.

verify: The token response contains access_token, refresh_token and id_token.
The JWKS at /realms/lab/protocol/openid-connect/certs lists the signing key.
Kill node 1: the session survives on node 2.
pitfalls: Issuer mismatch behind a proxy: set the public hostname correctly.
Missing audience mapper makes API aud checks fail.
Redirect URI wildcards that are too broad invite token theft.
Open 7800 and 57800 between nodes, or the cluster never forms.
Heap near the container limit gets the JVM OOM-killed.
Cache sessions are lost if every node restarts at once; roll nodes one by one.
Clock skew beyond the allowed leeway makes exp and nbf checks fail.
keyPoints: Authorization Code flow with PKCE signs users in once across every app.
Realms isolate users, clients and roles; roles become token claims.
APIs validate the JWT: signature, issuer, audience and expiry.
HA means Infinispan distributed caches plus one shared database.
quickDeploy: Install Keycloak behind TLS with PostgreSQL.
Create a realm, a public client with PKCE, and roles.
Run the code flow and inspect the JWT.
Add a second node and export the realm.
osiNote: Speaks HTTPS and OIDC; session state replicates between nodes on TCP 7800.
production: Run two or more nodes behind a load balancer with a shared database.
Size heap with MaxRAMPercentage; load test logins and watch GC pauses.
Export realms to JSON and keep them in Git.
Back up PostgreSQL and test the restore.
Alert on login errors, token endpoint p95 and cache cluster size.
